paper_title: Embodied AI Fails the Mirror Test: How a Simple Mirror Breaks Robot Policies

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Can a simple mirror expose the limitations of today's robotic manipulation policies? Inspired by the mirror self-recognition test in animal cognition, we investigate whether robot policies can reliably manipulate physical objects in scenes containing their reflections. We introduce RoboDojo-Mirror, a benchmark built on RoboDojo that preserves task objectives, success criteria, and policy checkpoints while comparing a mirror-free baseline with single-mirror, dual-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions. Across five policies spanning Vision-Language-Action models, World Action Models, and agentic policies, every mirror condition reduces aggregate success rates: averaged over the three conditions, the drop ranges from 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points across policies, and it reaches 62.5 points on the mirrored tabletop. Because a mirror is also a physical obstacle, we compare it against geometrically matched non-reflective panels; 50--88\% of mirror-specific failures occur without recorded robot--panel contact, so direct collisions alone do not explain the degradation. Trajectory and contact analyses instead reveal recurring behaviors consistent with phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real ones. Targeted diagnostics further characterize grasping near reflections, policy-dependent pushing progress, and physical-target interaction under main-camera occlusion. Real-robot experiments with $π_{0.5}$ and FastWAM also show lower overall success rates under the upright-mirror and mirrored-tabletop conditions. These findings reveal a shared vulnerability to reflective environments across diverse robot policies and motivate reflection-aware evaluation of embodied intelligence. Code is available at https://github.com/iPPLab/robodojo-mirror.

Introduction Can an ordinary mirror reveal limitations in how robots connect visual observations to physical actions? The classical mirror self-recognition test examines whether animals can use reflections to guide actions toward their own bodies [10]. Inspired by this behavioral probe, we ask whether robot policies can reliably locate and manipulate physical objects when their observations also contain reflections of those objects. Mirrors create structured discrepancy between visual appearance and actionable space. Reflections preserve recognizable features and change with physical objects, yet their apparent locations contain no additional manipulable targets. They can also adjoin real objects in images, forming composite contours, or reveal otherwise occluded targets. These properties enable tests of two complementary capabilities: maintaining reliable manipulation in the presence of reflections, and using reflected observations to act on occluded targets. Recent advances in generalist robot policies have expanded the range of manipulation tasks that can be performed from visual and language inputs, yet whether these policies possess the two capabilities above remains unclear. Vision-Language-Action models directly generate actions from multimodal observations, while World Action Models jointly model actions and future observations [2, 29]. Agentic policies provide another approach by selecting and invoking robot tools through repeated observation and reasoning [15]. However, strong performance under standard evaluation conditions does not establish robustness to changes in visual evidence. Controlled perturbation benchmarks have demonstrated substantial performance degradation under variations in viewpoints, lighting, backgrounds, and other conditions [7]. Reflections are not covered by these perturbations: rather than altering appearance, they duplicate task-relevant content at locations with known geometric relationship to the physical scene. Existing mirror-based evaluations have begun to examine embodied agents self-centric perception and selfinteraction, recognition [12]. We investigate different operational setting: generalist policies performing external-object manipuinspired by mirror including tasks lation under controlled mirror configurations. The question posed above breaks down into three parts: how reflections affect task completion, whether observed degradation extends beyond the effects of an inserted physical panel, and what execution behaviors accompany these changes. We introduce RoboDojo-Mirror, an evaluation benchmark built on RoboDojo [3]. As illustrated in Fig. 1, it preserves the original manipulation objectives and success criteria while evaluating policies under four conditions: no mirror, single mirror, dual mirrors, and mirrored tabletop. On shared set of eight tasks, we pair layouts and policy seeds across conditions to measure changes relative to each policys own mirror-free baseline. For selected policies, geometrically matched non-reflective panels provide additional controls for the effects of inserting physical structures. We further design three diagnostic scenarios, namely grasping on mirrored tabletop, pushing an object connected to its reflection, and acting with reflections as the main visual cue, combining task outcomes with trajectory and contact observations. This protocol enables researchers to assess reflection robustness using existing policies and task evaluators, and to characterize failures beyond aggregate success rates. Across five policies spanning Vision-Language-Action models, World Action Models, and agentic policies, all three mirror conditions reduce aggregate success rates, with average drops of 10.856.7 percentage points across policies. Matched panel comparisons show that 5088% of mirror-specific failures occur without recorded robotpanel contact, so direct collisions alone do not explain the degradation. The accompanying behaviors are consistent with phantom targeting of reflected objects and spatial mislocalization of real ones. The three diagnostics further show more frequent empty grasps, pushing progress that varies with policy and contour, and limited physical-target contact even with mirror-related hints. Real-robot experiments with π0.5 and FastWAM show similar overall degradation trend. Together, these results reveal shared vulnerability to reflections across diverse robot policies. 2. sections.title: Robustness
sections.content: Robotic manipulation benchmarks provide complementary tools for evaluating policy capabilities. LIBERO studlearning [20]. ies knowledge transfer in lifelong robot RoboTwin 2.0 combines scalable data generation with structured domain randomization for bimanual manipulation [4], while RoboDojo provides unified simulation and real-world evaluation framework for generalist manipulation policies [3]. Recent benchmarks place greater emphasis on robustness beyond nominal task success. LIBERO2 language, Plus introduces controlled perturbations to object layouts, camera viewpoints, robot initial states, lighting, backgrounds, and sensor observations [7]. LIBEROVPro evaluates closed-loop visual robustness by perturbing the evidence available during execution, including observation degradation, camera staleness, and cross-view consistency [17]. LIBERO-Pro2.0 further covers static and runtime shifts across environmental, observational, execution, robot-state, and language dimensions [35]. RoboPRO complements success-based evaluation with collision metrics under clutter and controlled perturbations [18]. Building on these evaluation principles, our work focuses on mirror-augmented manipulation, where reflections introduce structured visual ambiguity alongside physical scene changes. We evaluate task outcomes and contact behavior, and use geometrically matched non-reflective panels to examine performance differences beyond the presence of the panel itself. 2.2. Mirror Perception and Spatial Reasoning Mirrors challenge visual understanding because reflected objects can resemble directly observed objects while occupying different physical locations. Early mirror-detection methods identify reflective regions through contextual contrasts [28], while video-based approaches exploit spatial and temporal correspondences [19]. These methods address the localization of mirror regions rather than the action consequences of reflected observations. Mirror3D further estimates mirror geometry to refine unreliable depth measurements on reflective surfaces [26]. More recently, MIRA-Bench evaluates reflection-aware perception, spatial reasoning, and scene-level decisions in real RGB-D mirror scenes, exposing difficulties in reconciling reflected appearance with depth measurements [30]. MirrorQA examines subject-centered leftright reasoning in mirror contexts [21]. Related diagnostic benchmarks, including HallusionBench [11] and IllusionVQA [25], investigate visual illusions and failures of image-grounded reasoning. Unlike these perception-focused studies, we evaluate task outcomes and contact behavior during closed-loop manipulation under reflections. 2.3. Mirror-Mediated Robotic Interaction Robotic mirror research spans geometry and sensorimotor learning. Hart and Scassellati infer mirror viewpoints from learned sensorimotor relationships [14]. Marchand and Chaumette develop visual servoing for robot-mounted mirrors [22], while Lanillos et al. combine active inference and sensorimotor prediction for mirror self-recognition and self/other distinction [16]. Yoshioka et al. exploit mirror reflections to observe occluded regions, while UMI incorporates side mirrors for manipulation and shows that corrected mirror views can outperform uncorrected ones [6, 31]. Recent embodied evaluations extend mirror-based tests to multimodal agents. MirrorBench studies self-centric intelligence through simulated mirror interaction [12], while Ziliotto et al. evaluate whether agents can infer hidden selfattributes from reflections and use this evidence to guide actions [36]. Beyond self-centric tasks, Being-M0.7 evaluates mirror-assisted grasping of directly occluded toy in real-world humanoid task [33]. Our work studies reflection robustness across multiple generalist policies and manipulation tasks under controlled mirror configurations. 3. Benchmark Design and Evaluation Protocol Built on RoboDojo [3], RoboDojo-Mirror evaluates policy robustness to reflections while preserving the original task objectives and success criteria. Fig. 2 summarizes the paired evaluation protocol and controls. 3.1. Policy and Task Selection We evaluate five policies spanning Vision-LanguageAction models, World Action Models, and agentic policies: WALL-OSS-1.0-Lite (WALL-OSS) [27], VPP2 [13], Awomo-0.5 [1], Rex-M1 Preview [9], and GPT-6-Astra (Astra) [23, 34]. This selection covers different approaches to generating robot actions from visual observations. For open-weight policies, we use official checkpoints and inference configurations. Within each policy, we hold the checkpoint, observation interface, action interface, and inference settings fixed across scene conditions. For Astra, the available camera streams, robot-state interface, motion tools, and inference budget are likewise held fixed across conditions. We select shared eight-task set that balances diverse manipulation requirements with strong overall RoboDojo leaderboard performance. All policies are evaluated on under four conditions, using paired comparisons against their own mirror-free baselines. The tasks are listed in the supplementary material. 3.2. Mirror Configurations We construct four scene conditions from each task layout: no mirror, single vertical mirror, dual vertical mirrors, and mirrored tabletop. These conditions vary the placement and geometry of reflections while retaining matched initial object and robot states. No Mirror. We retain the original RoboDojo scene as the baseline. Single Mirror. vertical planar mirror is placed near tabletop edge, with its plane parallel to that edge and its reflective side facing the manipulation area. Dual Mirrors. Two vertical mirrors are placed along adjacent sides of the workspace, with mutually perpendicular planes and reflective faces oriented toward the manipulation area. This configuration introduces reflections from 3 Figure 2. Overview of the evaluation protocol in RoboDojo-Mirror. Policies are evaluated on matched task layouts under four scene conditions, with additional non-reflective panel controls for selected policies. both mirrors and may also show higher-order reflections, depending on visibility and rendering settings. Mirrored Tabletop. We replace the tabletops surface material with reflective finish while retaining its position and dimensions. Reflections therefore appear near the objects and the surface on which manipulation takes place. For the single-mirror and dual-mirror conditions, we shift the panels by 5 cm away from the robot relative to their initial construction positions, providing additional clearance while retaining visible reflections. The panels are fixed in the scene. This placement does not guarantee collisionfree execution; contact with the panels is therefore recorded separately from task success. For WALL-OSS and Awomo-0.5, we also replace the single and dual mirrors with geometry-matched nonreflective panels as physical-obstruction controls. No corresponding control is used for the mirrored tabletop. Across the four main evaluation conditions, we retain the original task instructions, matched initial object and robot states, and task success criteria. During scene validation, we inspect the camera streams supplied to each policy to check reflection visibility, direct target visibility, and initial intersections between the inserted panels and existing scene geometry. We retain the scene and camera configurations with the evaluation records. The target-occlusion experiments in Section 4.3 use separate diagnostic setup. 3.3. Evaluation Protocol and Metrics Paired Evaluation. For each policy and selected task, we run separate closed-loop episodes with matched layouts and policy seeds across scene conditions. The main evaluation uses five layouts and three policy seeds per task for WALLOSS, VPP2, Awomo-0.5, and Rex-M1 Preview. Astra uses five layouts with one rollout per layout. Termination and budgets. We retain the original task success criteria and task-specific termination rules. An episode ends when the task terminates or its execution budget is exhausted. Panel contact is recorded but is not an additional termination condition. For Astra, the execution budget also includes limit on model calls. Diagnostic experiments report their own layouts, seeds, and budgets when these differ from the main evaluation. Performance under Mirror Conditions Following Section 3, we report overall performance, mirrorpanel comparisons, targeted behavioral diagnostics, and real-world validation. Trajectory, video, and contact analyses characterize three observed behaviors: collision, phantom targeting, and spatial mislocalization. Collision. The robot contacts the mirror during execution, potentially disrupting manipulation. We distinguish such contact events from task failures, as contact does not necessarily cause failure. Phantom targeting. The robot directs manipulation actions toward reflected object rather than its physical counterpart, suggesting that the reflection is treated as an actionable target. Spatial mislocalization. The robot acts at an incorrect location relative to the physical target, resulting in missed grasps or ineffective manipulation without clear evidence of phantom targeting. 4.1. Overall Performance Table 1 reports task scores and success rates aggregated over the task set, with each policy compared against its own mirror-free baseline. All five policies achieve mirror-free success rates of 60.872.5%, and every mirror configuration reduces their aggregate success rates. The average paired SR drops range from 10.8 to 56.7 percentage points across policies. With mirrored tabletop, VPP2 drops from 72.5% to 27.5%, while Rex-M1 Preview drops from 66.7% to 4.2%. Task scores also decrease under all mirror configurations. Overall, dual mirrors tend to cause greater performance degradation than single mirrors, with VPP2 as an exception. WALL-OSS and Awomo-0.5 reach their lowest success rates under dual mirrors, whereas VPP2, Rex-M1 Preview, and Astra perform worst with mirrored tabletop. Astra shows little aggregate change under single mirror (65.0% to 62.5%), but its SR decreases to 52.5% under dual mirrors and 47.5% with mirrored tabletop. Despite the highest recorded robotmirror contact rates under single and dual mirrors (55.0% and 85.0%), Astra exhibits relatively small SR drops, suggesting that contact occurrence alone does not explain performance degradation. Since execution budgets differ across policies, these aggregates should not be interpreted as controlled crosspolicy ranking. Furthermore, task outcomes alone cannot separate visual interference from physical obstruction, motivating the mirrorpanel comparisons in the next subsection. 4.2. Real-World Validation To examine whether the performance degradation observed in simulation extends to physical manipulation, we evaluate robot policies under real-world mirror conditions. We evaluate π0.5 [24] and FastWAM [32] on Franka robot across four tasks: produce placement, block stacking, bracket flipping, and cylinder insertion. Each task uses no-mirror, upright-mirror, and mirrored-tabletop conditions  (Fig. 6)  . The upright condition uses single vertical mirror, matching the simulated single-mirror configuration in type. Five matched initial layouts with two repetitions each yield 10 trials per task, policy, and condition. Checkpoints, instructions, camera configurations, and execution budgets remain fixed across conditions. Further experimental details are provided in the supplementary material. Table 6 shows lower overall SR under both mirror conditions. For π0.5, SR decreases from 77.5% without mirrors to 52.5% with an upright mirror and 27.5% with mirrored tabletop; FastWAM decreases from 60.0% to 30.0% and 10.0%, respectively. Both policies achieve 80.0% on block stacking without mirrors but 0.0% with mirrored tabletop. These results show an overall degradation trend consistent with simulation. 5. Paired evaluations across five policies and real-world experiments show lower success rates under mirrors. sections.title: Overview
sections.content: This supplementary material documents scene geometry, policy configurations, and evaluation metrics (Appendix A); task-level results (Appendix B); mirrorpanel controls and contact measurements (Appendix C); tabletop grasping, Push-T, and target-occlusion diagnostics (Appendices D, E, and F); and real-world deployment details (Appendix G). A. Scene Geometry and Evaluation Details A.1. Mirror Geometry and Virtual Images Two mirrors can produce both first-order images, formed by single reflection, and higher-order images, formed by successive reflections between the mirrors. Figure 7 illustrates the virtual-image arrangements for three idealized mirror configurations. The illustrated 90, 60, and 45 configurations produce three, five, and seven virtual images, respectively. Our main dual-mirror evaluation uses perpendicular mirrors (90). The other angles illustrate reflection geometry rather than additional evaluated conditions. In the experimental scenes, finite mirror dimensions, camera viewpoints, occlusion, and rendering settings determine which virtual images are actually visible in the policy observations. A.2. Policy Configurations We evaluate four pretrained robot policies: WALL-OSS1.0-Lite, VPP2, Awomo-0.5, and Rex-M1 Preview, together with the tool-using GPT-6-Astra agent. For the four pretrained policies, we use their officially released checkpoints and corresponding inference configurations, without addiFigure 7. Idealized virtual-image arrangements for two mirrors with included angles of (a) 90, (b) 60, and (c) 45. Solid red markers denote the physical object; filled pale markers denote first-order images; outlined markers denote higher-order images. The diagrams illustrate reflection geometry, not camera-visible image counts. 1 tional training or mirror-specific adaptation. Within each policy, we keep the checkpoint, observation preprocessing, camera inputs, action representation, and inference settings fixed across scene conditions. Task instructions and native success criteria are likewise preserved. The scene condition is not supplied as an additional policy input in the main evaluation. The mirror-related instruction variants are restricted to the target-occlusion diagnostic. Policy-specific inference and control settings are retained rather than forced into common action interface. Consequently, comparisons primarily measure changes relative to each policys own mirror-free baseline. GPT-6Astra additionally uses an explicit robot-tool interface and decision-call budget, as detailed below. Table 7 summarizes the policy configurations. Prediction horizon denotes the number of action steps generated per inference, while replanning interval denotes the number executed before requesting new prediction. WALL-OSS uses selective BF16 parameter casting while retaining FP32 components. Awomo-0.5 uses the original RoboDojo checkpoint. VPP2 uses the RoboDojo EE16 deployment adapter; the checkpoint name does not indicate the executed action representation. GPT-6-Astra selects individual motion-tool actions with variable execution duration, rather than predicting fixed-length action chunks. Its reasoning effort is set to medium, which is distinct from numerical precision. A.2.1. GPT-6-Astra Agent Configuration tool-using We configure GPT-6-Astra as closed-loop, agent with the RoboDojo Inspect-EEF interface. We access the model through the Codex CLIs app-server interface using ChatGPT subscription authentication, rather than direct, API-key-authenticated access to the OpenAI API. The model is requested as gpt-6-astra with reasoning effort set to medium. At each observation boundary, it receives RGB images from the head camera and both wrist cameras, robot proprioceptive state, and execution feedback. Depth observations and simulator ground-truth object coordinates are not provided. The agent uses two tools. move eef specifies worldframe end-effector position, orientation, and gripper opening for one or both arms. The native executor validates the targets, plans joint trajectories with cuRobo, and executes them through the simulators robot controller. The agent subsequently receives execution feedback and updated observations. The give up tool allows the agent to terminate an unsuccessful attempt. EE denotes end-effector pose and gripper targets; Joint denotes joint-position and gripper targets. Horizons and replanning intervals are measured in control steps. Turn the white plastic bracket upside down. Insert the cylindrical object into the circular holder. G.2. Tasks and Mirror Placement We consider four tabletop manipulation tasks: produce placement, block stacking, bracket flipping, and cylinder insertion. Table 23 lists the task instructions recorded in the deployment documentation. Each task is evaluated under three scene conditions: no mirror, an upright mirror, and mirrored tabletop. The upright mirror introduces reflected views beside the physical workspace. The mirrored tabletop introduces reflections near the objects and their supporting surface. Representative configurations and task initial states are shown in Fig. 6. For bracket flipping, the original instruction is retained verbatim. Following the recorded demonstrations, success is defined as reaching stable upright configuration. G.3. Execution and Recording Protocol For each task and policy, we evaluate the same five initial layouts across the three scene conditions, with two repetitions per layout. This yields 10 trials per task, policy, and condition. Table 6 reports the corresponding task-level success rates. Within each policy, we use the same checkpoint, task instruction, and camera configuration across scene conditions. Each policy uses its own deployment interface and action rate. Success criteria. We assess task success using the following criteria: Produce placement: The produce is fully placed inside the basket and released by the gripper. Block stacking: The red block is placed on the blue block and remains stable for at least 3 after gripper release. Figure 13. Target-occlusion setup and instruction variants for cover blocks. An elevated panel occludes the physical targets from the main camera while preserving their mirror reflections. The oblique view illustrates the physical arrangement; it is not an additional policy camera. Brief and Detailed add the corresponding prefixes to the original task instruction. G. Real-World Experimental Details G.1. Robot, Cameras, and Policy Configurations We use Franka FR3 manipulator equipped with paralleljaw gripper. Visual observations are provided by two Intel RealSense D435i cameras: fixed external camera overlooking the workspace and wrist-mounted camera. Both cameras capture RGB images at 640 480 resolution and 30 Hz. Depth, infrared, and inertial streams are disabled in the camera configuration. The policy input includes the two RGB views and an eight-dimensional proprioceptive state: seven measured joint positions in radians and the total gripper width in metres. The deployed action interface contains seven absolute joint-position targets and binary gripper command, where 0 denotes opening and 1 denotes grasping. Commands are executed through the ROS 2 joint-impedance control stack. We use Franka-specific checkpoints for both π0.5 and FastWAM. The π0.5 deployment uses LoRA-adapted multitask checkpoint at training step 31,927, with 32-step prediction horizon and 15 Hz action grid. FastWAM uses the multitask checkpoint at training step 30,000, with 64-step prediction horizon and 30 Hz action grid. Each checkpoint is paired with its saved normalization statistics. For π0.5, camera images are processed at 224 224 resolution. For FastWAM, the client forwards the separate native-resolution images to the server, which applies the checkpoints training-compatible image preprocessing. Figure 14. The shared initial views show the occluder in the main camera and directly visible physical targets in the right-wrist camera. The Original execution succeeds at control step 463, and the Brief execution ends without success at step 800. Numbers below the images give the recorded control steps. and denote the left and right wrist cameras. Bracket flipping: The bracket is turned from its initial lying pose to stable upright configuration. Cylinder insertion: The cylinder is stably seated in the receiving container and released by the gripper. Trial scoring. For canceled recordings, we determine task outcomes from the available execution and termination records. Policy-related command rejections, controller alarms, and safety stops count as failures. Such trials remain in the denominator of 10 trials per task, policy, and condition.
